rights.title: If the police arrest you
rights.lede: Arrest is not punishment. The law gives you rights from the first minute, and the police must follow them.
rights.point: You must be told why you are being arrested, and, if the offence is bailable, that you can be released on bail.

rights.title: Filing an FIR
rights.lede: For a cognizable offence (theft, assault, cheating and the like), the police must record your complaint. Here is how, and what to do if they refuse.
rights.point: You can report at any police station, wherever the offence happened (a "zero FIR"). It is then sent to the right station.

rights.title: Bail, in plain words
rights.lede: Bail lets you stay free while the case goes on. Whether it is a right or the court's choice depends on the offence.
rights.point: For a bailable offence, bail is your right. The police or court must release you once you give bail or a bond.

rights.title: Consumer complaints
rights.lede: A faulty product, a service not given, an unfair charge: you can take it to a Consumer Commission yourself, without a lawyer.
rights.point: File in the District Commission for claims up to ₹50 lakh (the limit set in 2021). Bigger claims go to the State or National Commission.

rights.title: Renting a home
rights.lede: Rent law is mostly state law, so details vary. These points hold across India.
rights.point: A lease for a year or more must be in writing and registered. That is why many agreements are for 11 months.

rights.title: Domestic violence
rights.lede: Abuse at home is not only physical. The law protects women against physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse.
rights.point: Cruelty by a husband or his relatives, including harassment for dowry, is a crime.

rights.title: When a cheque bounces
rights.lede: A bounced cheque for a debt is a criminal offence, but the deadlines are strict. Miss one and the case can fail.
rights.point: Send a written demand notice to the person who gave the cheque within 30 days of the bank's return memo.

rights.title: Sexual harassment at work
rights.lede: Every workplace with ten or more employees must have an Internal Committee to hear complaints. Smaller ones are covered by a Local Committee.
rights.point: Complain in writing to the Internal Committee within three months of the incident (or the last one). The Committee can extend this by three months.

rights.title: Free legal aid
rights.lede: The Constitution promises justice that doesn't depend on money. Legal Services Authorities give free lawyers and advice to many people.
rights.point: The State must make sure no one is denied justice for lack of money, and provide free legal aid.

guides.title: Money lost to an online fraud
guides.lede: UPI, card, bank or investment scam. The first hour matters most: money can often be frozen before it moves on.

guides.title: Someone close to you was arrested
guides.lede: What to do in the first hours, and the rights the person has from the moment of arrest.

guides.title: The police won't register your FIR
guides.lede: For a cognizable offence (theft, assault, cheating and the like), registering an FIR is the police's duty. Here's the ladder if they refuse.

guides.title: A cheque given to you bounced
guides.lede: A bounced cheque can be a criminal case, but only if you keep to strict time limits. Miss one and the case can fail.

guides.title: You were in a road accident
guides.lede: Care first, then the paperwork that decides compensation. There is a six-month limit on claims.

guides.title: You received a legal notice
guides.lede: A notice is a demand, not a court order. Don't ignore it, and don't panic: read it, note the deadline, and reply carefully.

guides.title: You face violence at home
guides.lede: Your safety comes first. The law protects you from physical, emotional, sexual and financial abuse, and from being thrown out of your home.

guides.title: Landlord keeping your deposit or forcing you out
guides.lede: A landlord can end a tenancy only by proper notice and, if you don't leave, through a court. Locking you out or cutting the water is not the way.

guides.title: A product or service let you down
guides.lede: Defective goods, a service not delivered, a refund refused. Consumer Commissions are cheap, need no lawyer, and you can file online.

templates.title: RTI application
templates.blurb: Ask any public authority for information under the Right to Information Act, 2005.

templates.title: Consumer complaint
templates.blurb: A complaint to the District Consumer Commission about a defective product or deficient service.

templates.title: Cheque bounce notice
templates.blurb: The demand notice under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act that must go out before any case.

templates.title: Rent agreement (11 months)
templates.blurb: A plain residential leave-and-licence style rent agreement for up to 11 months.

templates.title: Police complaint (to register an FIR)
templates.blurb: A written complaint to the officer in charge of a police station asking for an FIR under Section 173 of the BNSS.

templates.title: RTI first appeal
templates.blurb: Appeal to the First Appellate Authority when an RTI reply is late, incomplete or refused.

templates.title: Security deposit refund notice
templates.blurb: A firm written demand to your landlord to return your security deposit after you've moved out.

templates.title: Unpaid salary notice
templates.blurb: A written demand to a former or current employer for unpaid salary or final settlement dues.

templates.title: Legal aid application (free lawyer)
templates.blurb: Ask the District Legal Services Authority for a free lawyer under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
